newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-KUERTEN LEFT SANDY BEACHES TO SHINE ON PARIS CLAY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KUERTEN LEFT SANDY BEACHES TO SHINE ON PARIS CLAY.

text.p: They don't play tennis on the beach in Rio but if they did, Gustavo Kuerten would probably be Copacabana's favourite.
The 20-year-old Kuerten, who became the first Brazilian to reach a grand slam semifinal at the French Open on Tuesday, is a keen surfer and, of course, a football lover.
But his favourite sport cannot be performed on sand.

"Like all Brazilians I played football but I found the ball was too big," he said. "I also love surfing, even if I'm not that good at it. At the age of 14 I decided I wanted to be a tennis professional and when I was 17 I started to work real hard to become one."

Kuerten, who is ranked a modest 66th in the world and has won only one tournament on the Challenger circuit in Curitiba, Brazil, was regarded merely as an exotic attraction when the Paris event started.
But he has delighted the crowds here with his unpredictable and spectacular game, beating proven clay-court experts such as Austrian Thomas Muster and Ukraine's Andrei Medvedev.
On Tuesday, he went on to knock out holder Yevgeny Kafelnikov of Russia in five sets and advance to the last four.
"My wins against Muster and Medvedev boosted my confidence," he said. "I said to myself 'Why not Kafelnikov?'."
Kuerten now faces a player ranked below him, Belgian Filip Dewulf, 122nd in the world, in a surreal semifinal showdown.
"Obviously I'm suprised to be in the semifinals," he said. "I've never played that well and I've got nothing to lose."
Kuerten, whose flashy yellow-and-blue outfit evokes the colours of the Brazilian soccer team, was asked by the French Open organisers to wear more traditional clothes.
"The problem is I don't have anything else," he said. "The only white thing I've got is my underwear."
'Guga', as his friends call him, is of German descent and likes to talk about his German grandmother Olga, who is his number one fan.
"She knows all the great players and she gives me good advice," he said.
But apart from that he is every bit Brazilian.
"I don't speak a word of German," said Kuerten, who has long, curly black hair and is growing a beard. "I stopped shaving after winning in Curitiba, just before coming here. It's for luck."
Kuerten turned serious at his post-match press conference when asked to talk about his father, who died when he was eight years old.
"I dedicate my whole life to him," he said. "He was a great person."

But the smile returned when he was asked if he would celebrate his victory over Kafelnikov. Kuerten said he would simply watch television: "There's a football match, France are playing Brazil. I hope we'll win."
